title: EuroTrip
synopsis: Graduation week. A penpal in Berlin. Three friends, one rail pass, and an unwise budget. The plane lands in London at 6 a.m. Go.

nodes.text: Six a.m. at Heathrow with two backpacks too many, because Cooper packed a second backpack for his first backpack. Scott has the rail pass in a neck pouch he will not stop touching. Jenny has the itinerary in a binder. The binder says DAY 1: LONDON. The plan, written nowhere in that binder, is Mieke.

choices.consequence: You give England forty hours. Cooper spends nine of them explaining to a barman that he is technically not the same as other Americans. You start with London. It gets you to The Hostel, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You're at the train before the jet lag lands. Jenny's binder loses page four in a turnstile and she never mentions it again. You commit to skip to Paris. The road to The Hostel is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Vinnie runs the hostel and calls everyone 'my friend' with a small pause before it. There's one bathroom, a laminated sign about the bathroom, and a house rule involving the word 'donations.' Your room sleeps eleven. Nine of them are asleep at four in the afternoon. Vinnie says that's normal. Vinnie says a lot of things are normal.

choices.consequence: You hand Vinnie your passports for 'registration.' He puts them in a drawer with six other passports and most of a sandwich. You commit to trust Vinnie. The road to Hooligans is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You sleep in your shoes with the backpack as a pillow. In the morning everything you own is where you left it and your neck is ruined. You choose to sleep with one eye open. By Hooligans, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Scott, four pints in, says the words 'it's only a game' to a man with a tattoo of a stadium on his forearm. The pub goes quiet in a wave, table by table. Somebody's grandmother stands up. You are out the door before Scott finishes his apology, which he is still delivering over one shoulder, at a sprint.

choices.consequence: Scott buys the whole table a round with money you needed for Wednesday. They forgive him instantly, then teach him a chant about Cooper. You choose to apologize. By Channel Crossing, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You do nine blocks in bad shoes and lose them at a kebab window. Cooper, wheezing against a bin, calls it the best night of his life. You outrun them. It gets you to Channel Crossing, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: The Channel is doing something the ferry brochure never mentioned. Cooper has gone a green that seems medically interesting, gripping the rail, apologizing out loud to the sea. Jenny holds his backpack. Scott films it. You learn that travel friendship is mostly this: standing near somebody at their absolute worst and not making it a thing.

choices.consequence: You get him crackers and a window seat and carry his bag for two hours. He will bring this up in a wedding speech someday. You choose to take care of Cooper. By Paris, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You sit upwind with a paperback and let Jenny handle it. Cooper notices. Cooper notices everything and files it alphabetically. You choose to read on deck. By Paris, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Paris does the thing where it refuses to be overrated. You eat a four-euro sandwich sitting on a curb and it quietly rearranges your understanding of bread. Scott says 'wow' six times in one block. You are nineteen, you smell like a train, and you have never been more precisely the right age for anything.

choices.consequence: Six hundred and sixty-nine steps, because the lift queue was ninety minutes. Cooper counts them aloud. The entire stairwell learns Cooper's name.

Three hours and one coffee, watching a street work. The waiter respects this. The waiter respects nothing else about any of you. You choose to sit in a cafe. By Mime, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: The mime attaches himself outside a church and will not be un-attached. He does the box. He does a devastating impression of Scott that Jenny cannot stop laughing at. When you finally shake him at midnight, he presses a card into your hand. There's a phone number on it. The card is real. He is a mime with a business.

choices.consequence: He rides three trains with you and never once speaks. Jenny gives him half a sandwich. He mimes eating it, then actually eats it. You choose to keep the mime. By Amsterdam, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You give him two euros and a handshake. He mimes weeping. For all you know he is behind that church still doing it. You choose to tip the mime, move on. By Amsterdam, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Canals, bicycles, and a man named Hennie who runs 'tours' out of a doorway with a laminated sign and no discernible route. The tour lasts ninety minutes and covers four bars and his ex-wife. Cooper takes notes. Cooper takes notes on all of it, in a little pad, like it's going to be on a test.

choices.consequence: Twelve euros each. You see one windmill, two bars, and the apartment where Hennie's marriage ended. Somehow, worth it. You take the tour. It gets you to Rome, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You get lost for four hours and finish at a herring cart. Scott eats a whole raw fish on a dare worth exactly one euro. You choose to wander on your own. By Rome, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Rome on a Saturday is a carnival that has been running for two thousand years and does not require your attendance. The Trevi has rules: one coin, right hand, over the left shoulder, or it doesn't count. Scott has one coin left in the world. That coin is also, technically, dinner.

choices.consequence: He throws it wrong-handed and it lands on a tourist's hat. The wish stands, Jenny rules. You split three plates of pasta four ways. You choose to throw the coin. By The Train Station Pickpocket, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

Scott pockets it and buys a slice of pizza with it an hour later. He looks back at the fountain the entire time he's eating. You choose to save the coin. By The Train Station Pickpocket, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Termini, platform nine. A man in a very good coat bumps Scott, apologizes beautifully in three languages, and walks off with the wallet. Scott — who has never been coordinated at anything, ever — jogs after him, bumps him back, and returns holding the wallet. Nobody present, Scott included, knows how that happened.

choices.consequence: You buy him a beer he can now afford. He retells it four times by Tuesday and the coat gets nicer in every version. You commit to celebrate. The road to Vatican Robbed is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.
Scott jogs back and hands the man his own wallet, which he also somehow has. The man is genuinely moved. Neither mentions the exchange rate.

nodes.text: A guard in the colonnade takes Scott gently by the elbow. There is, it turns out, an Australian with the same haircut who owes a Roman hotel eleven hundred euros. The guard is polite. The guard has a photograph. In the photograph, honestly, it is Scott. Jenny leans in, studies it, and agrees out loud that it's Scott.

choices.consequence: Jenny does four minutes of confident, wrong Italian. It works. The guard mostly wants to get back to standing in the shade. You explain. It gets you to Berlin, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.
You run inside the most famous church on earth, which the guard correctly identifies as a strategic error. He collects you at the gift shop.

nodes.text: Berlin in August is doing eleven degrees and taking it personally. Mieke's address turns out to be a real street, a real building, a real buzzer with a real surname beside it. Scott has been carrying this address for six weeks. He looks at the buzzer. Nobody presses the buzzer. The four of you stand there like a delivery.

choices.consequence: Scott knocks with two knuckles, badly, twice. Then steps back and fixes his hair with a hand that is visibly shaking. You commit to knock. The road to Mieke is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You lose ninety minutes to courage in a bar across the street. The bartender, unprompted, tells Scott to go and ring the bell. You wait at the bar. It gets you to Mieke, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: She opens the door in socks. She is taller than six weeks of imagining allowed, she says Scott's name like it's an ordinary word, and she has clearly not been informed that four Americans were coming. Behind her someone turns the music down. She looks at all of you and says, 'So.

choices.consequence: Scott explains the entire email situation in one long sentence with no breathing in it. She lets him finish. Then she laughs. You commit to apologize for the misunderstanding. The road to Berghain (parody version) is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

Scott attempts a line he has been rehearsing since Amsterdam. It lands at about sixty percent, which is sixty more than anyone predicted. You choose to try to charm her. By Berghain (parody version), the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: The doorman is a large, calm man who has decided several things about you in under a second. He takes Jenny. He does not take the rest of you. No explanation is offered; none has ever been offered to anyone. Jenny mouths 'sorry' through the door and is swallowed by fog and a bass note you can feel in your teeth.

choices.consequence: Three hours on a curb with one shared bag of crisps. She comes out at five a.m. glowing and refuses, forever, to describe any of it. You wait outside for Jenny. It gets you to Train, Overnight, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You find a place with a fog machine and nine customers. Cooper wins a dance-off against a man twice his size and never explains the rules. You choose to find another club. By Train, Overnight, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Night train to Bratislava, second class, which is a shelf with a curtain of aspiration. The compartment smells of sausage and other people's socks. Cooper is asleep in ninety seconds, upright, mouth open, entirely at peace. You lie on your shelf listening to Scott not sleeping on the shelf above you.

choices.consequence: You take the corridor floor with a sweater for a pillow and wake with a boot print on your shin. Best sleep of the trip. You sleep on the floor. It gets you to Bratislava, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You and Scott talk to Vienna about nothing, then about Mieke, then about his dad. At dawn neither of you mentions it again. You choose to stay up all night. By Bratislava, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Your guidebook said 'affordable.' Your guidebook was written by a coward. Dinner for four — soup, dumplings, a plate of meat with its own architecture, four beers — costs less than one Paris sandwich. The waiter keeps bringing things nobody ordered and refusing to charge for them. Cooper cries a little, at the table, into a dumpling.

choices.consequence: You book two more nights on the strength of the dumplings alone. It is the only decision this entire trip that nobody argues about. You stay an extra day. It gets you to Robot Club, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You leave in the morning with leftovers wrapped in a napkin. Cooper carries that napkin across two borders like a holy relic. You commit to move on. The road to Robot Club is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: The bar advertises a robot bartender. The robot bartender pours a beer, hits a pose, and has a small wet patch of sweat on its silver forehead. His name is Tomas. He has done nine hours in the suit today. He is, movement-wise, an excellent robot and, spiritually, a man who needs to sit down.

choices.consequence: You buy Tomas a drink he can't get through the helmet. He takes his break at your table and talks about his daughter for forty minutes. You choose to befriend the man. By Italian Train Chaos, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You applaud the robot sincerely and tip it. Tomas performs a small bow that is, unmistakably, grateful in an extremely human way. You commit to pretend you didn't notice. The road to Italian Train Chaos is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: The strike is announced by a man with a megaphone and confirmed by everyone lying down. You sleep in the station under a departure board that updates all night to say nothing. A stray dog surveys your group, walks the whole row of you, and lies down on Cooper. Not near Cooper. On him.

choices.consequence: You name him Ferrovia and feed him half a panino. He follows you to the platform and stops at the yellow line like a professional. You adopt the dog. It gets you to Pope Audience, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You spend nine euros each on a room with one bed and a fan. Cooper sleeps on the floor anyway, out of loyalty to the dog. You choose to find a hotel. By Pope Audience, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: You're in the square for the wrong reason — shade — when the crowd tightens and a small white figure comes down the aisle. He stops. Of the many thousand people present, he puts a hand on Cooper's head. Cooper, raised Lutheran, has no protocol whatsoever for this.

choices.consequence: Jenny gets the shot: Cooper mid-blessing, face doing something between joy and panic. It stays his profile picture for nine years. You choose to take a photo. By Mieke, Again, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

Nobody reaches for a camera. Afterwards none of you can prove it happened, which somehow makes Cooper tell it better. You just be there. It gets you to Mieke, Again, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Mieke turns up in Venice with a backpack and no advance notice, which is the most Mieke thing available. She and Scott spend the whole boat ride arguing about a band. Halfway across the water Scott stops mid-sentence, looks at the wake, and works out — five weeks and four countries late — what is happening to him.

choices.consequence: You take Cooper and Jenny for gelato nobody wanted and leave those two alone on a bridge for two hours. It costs you nine euros. You choose to step back graciously. By Last Night, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You start a running bit about Scott's lagoon epiphany that outlives four apartments, two weddings, and one very inappropriate funeral. You joke about it forever. It gets you to Last Night, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Lisbon, hostel bar, four euros left between the group. Somebody two tables over is playing guitar badly and nobody minds. Jenny does the count out loud: nine countries, three arrests that weren't arrests, one dog. Nobody says the word 'ending.' Everybody orders one more anyway, which is how you say it without saying it.

choices.consequence: You stand up and give a speech with no structure and one genuinely good line about Cooper. Scott is crying by sentence three. You toast everyone. It gets you to Heathrow Again, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You say nothing and let the guitar handle it. On the walk back Jenny bumps your shoulder once, and that covers everything. You choose to just enjoy. By Heathrow Again, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Same terminal, same fluorescent hum, ten weeks and one lifetime later. Your backpack weighs less and smells considerably worse. Cooper falls asleep at the gate holding a napkin from Bratislava. You are, on paper, the identical person who landed here in June, and you are lying about that directly to a passport officer's face.

choices.consequence: You board. Somewhere over the Atlantic, Cooper says 'so, next summer,' and four people with no money whatsoever immediately say yes. You commit to go home. The road to Senior Year is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You let them board without you and buy a train ticket you can't afford. Jenny passes forty euros through the barrier and won't discuss it. You choose to stay one more week. By One More Week, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You change one flight and follow Scott back to Berlin, on the grounds that somebody has to be there to witness this. You commit to take the third path. The road to Berlin, Forever is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: You go home. Senior year starts and you are marginally harder to impress. The trip becomes the unit of measurement — 'that's nothing, in Bratislava we—' — and your roommates learn to leave the room. Ten years on, at somebody's kitchen island, four adults who now own printers and opinions about mattresses will do the mime's box routine until a spouse asks them, kindly, to stop.

One week becomes five. You wash dishes in a Lisbon hostel in exchange for a bunk and learn nine words of Portuguese, six of them useless. You miss the first two weeks of senior year and an internship that does not wait. On the flight home you finally understand the thing nobody tells you: it's still there. It'll keep being there. You can come back. You will, twice.

Scott marries Mieke four years later in a Berlin function room with regrettable carpet. You're best man. Your toast runs nineteen minutes and includes a slide. Cooper does the mime bit at the reception and a German cousin films the whole thing. Somewhere in the middle you stop performing and just say that you were standing there the night he knocked on that door. Everyone cries. The DJ waits.
